**Vignette: Elena, Age 39**

Elena is a 39-year-old dentist of Polish descent who has been practicing for over a decade in a busy urban clinic. She lives with her long-term partner, Marek, in a flat they share near the city center. From the outside, her life looks composed and purposeful — a capable professional, a devoted partner, someone who has always prided herself on being the steady one in any room.

Two years ago, Elena noticed a lump beneath her jaw that she initially dismissed as a swollen lymph node. As someone who spends her days examining heads and necks, she was familiar enough with anatomy to rationalize the finding — and, she now admits, to avoid looking too closely. When a colleague finally persuaded her to see her GP, the referral chain moved quickly. Within six weeks she had a diagnosis: Hodgkin's lymphoma, stage two. She was thirty-seven years old and had never been seriously ill a day in her life.

The months of chemotherapy that followed dismantled her sense of herself in ways she had not anticipated. She had always associated her identity with competence and precision — the steadiness of her hands, the control she exercised over her clinical environment. Treatment stripped that away. She was nauseated, exhausted, and frightened in a way she describes as unlike anything she has ever known — not fear of pain exactly, but a constant, low-frequency terror that her body had become a place she could no longer trust. There was one night, midway through her third cycle, when her fever spiked and she was admitted to hospital at two in the morning. She genuinely believed she might not leave. That night sits at the center of everything that has followed.

Elena completed treatment fourteen months ago and her oncologist considers her in remission. By most external measures, she has recovered. She returned to work, resumed her routines, and receives regular monitoring scans. But the scans themselves have become a source of dread that builds for weeks beforehand. She lies awake the night before appointments running through worst-case scenarios with a thoroughness she recognizes as irrational but cannot interrupt. When results come back clear, the relief lasts perhaps two days before the cycle begins again.

At work, she functions well in most respects, but she has noticed that she now responds differently when patients present with unusual oral lesions or unexplained swelling. Where she was once methodical and calm, she now feels a tight, urgent anxiety rise in her chest — not just clinical concern, but something that feels personal and out of proportion. She has caught herself overexplaining to patients, perhaps trying to spare them the shock she was not spared herself.

At home, Marek has been patient and loving, but Elena is aware that she keeps a certain distance from him that was not there before. She struggles to fully inhabit moments of happiness — a quiet evening, a holiday they took last summer — because somewhere beneath the surface runs the thought that this could all be taken from her. She does not tell him this. She does not want to burden him, and she is also not entirely sure she could find the words.

Her sleep is fragmented. She wakes most nights between three and four in the morning and cannot return to sleep, her mind moving restlessly through memories of the hospital — the sound of the IV pump, the particular quality of light in the ward at night, the face of the nurse who sat with her during that frightening admission. She does not consider herself a dramatic person, and this is part of what troubles her: she is well, she survived, she is grateful. She cannot fully account for why her nervous system continues to behave as though the danger has not passed.

She has not spoken to anyone professionally about any of this until now. She made the appointment, she says, because she is tired of waiting to feel like herself again.
